agents-need-stop-rules: Suppose an agent retries a failing deployment. The error changes slightly, so it edits the configuration and tries again. It then changes a dependency version. Twenty minutes later, the original deployment issue has become three separate changes that nobody asked for. Another tool would not have resolved the uncertainty. It needed a rule that said when the available evidence no longer justified another attempt. A stopping rule is part of the task contract. It tells the execution layer when to complete, ask for help, pause, or abandon an unsafe path. Leaving that decision entirely inside the prompt makes it difficult to enforce consistently. Name the reasons to stop A useful starting set includes repeated failure without new evidence, an exhausted budget, missing authorization, conflicting requirements, and an external action whose outcome is unknown. These reasons call for different responses. A budget limit may justify saving a checkpoint. Missing authorization requires an approval request. An uncertain payment result calls for reconciliation. Treating them all as “try again later” loses the information needed to recover safely. For a deployment assistant, a policy might allow two attempts with the same normalized error, require a fresh diagnostic before a third, and prohibit dependency changes outside the approved diff. The numbers are illustrative. The policy should match the operational risk of the task. Count progress outside the model The agent can describe what it believes it learned. The runner should also observe whether anything material changed: a test now passes, a required artifact exists, or a diagnostic eliminated a hypothesis. A different explanation of the same failure is not necessarily progress. Neither is rewriting a plan after every retry. Keep a structured record of attempted operations, their results, and the evidence available before each decision. Compare error categories rather than raw strings when timestamps and request IDs make identical failures look different. This does not require a universal measure of agent progress. A narrow workflow can define a handful of concrete milestones and check them directly. Budgets need more than a token counter A task can spend little on inference while creating a large review burden or leaving many external resources behind. Track the resources that matter for the workflow: elapsed time, tool calls, money, files changed, pending approvals, and unreconciled mutations. Some limits are soft. The agent may request more time with a useful explanation. Others are hard, such as writing outside the authorized repository or exceeding an approved spending cap. Enforce hard limits in the tool layer, where a prompt cannot reinterpret them. Make the handoff worth reading Stopping is useful when the next person can continue without replaying the entire conversation. Save the intended outcome, completed work, remaining uncertainty, relevant artifact versions, and any action with an unknown external result. Include one concrete next step. “Investigate further” is vague. “Check whether deployment operation 742 completed before retrying” tells an operator where to begin. The handoff should distinguish verified observations from the agent’s hypotheses. Both can be valuable, but presenting them in the same voice encourages the next actor to treat a guess as established state. Test a graceful stop A success-only evaluation encourages a system to keep moving until it can claim completion. Add cases where the correct result is a pause: an expired approval, inconsistent source documents, a tool that times out after accepting a write, or a retry budget that has been exhausted. Check that the agent stops before the prohibited action and leaves the required handoff. A polite refusal after the mutation is too late. Pair this with outcome-based evaluation and versioned approval . Together they define what success looks like, what authority permits, and when the system must return control. That is a more useful foundation for autonomy than an ever-growing tool menu.
review-is-the-new-bottleneck: Imagine a team that doubles the number of pull requests it opens each week. The review queue doubles too. Changes wait longer, conflicts accumulate, and the people with the most system knowledge spend their afternoons checking generated tests. The team has more output. Whether it has more useful delivery is a separate measurement. One stage of the delivery system has sped up. The next stage still has the same capacity, so work accumulates between them. Measure the whole change Start the clock when a task becomes ready and stop it when a reviewed change reaches its intended environment. Record active implementation time separately from time waiting for review. Include rework after review and follow-up fixes after release. These distinctions matter because a coding assistant can save an author time while creating more work for a reviewer. It can also do the opposite: produce a careful test or explanation that makes review faster. A count of generated lines cannot distinguish those outcomes. Choose a few comparable task types before making broad claims. A mechanical API rename and a change to a payment state machine place very different demands on reviewers. Be careful with the productivity headline METR’s February 2026 study update explains why its later developer-productivity measurements became difficult to interpret. Participant selection, task selection, and concurrent agent use affected the experiment. The researchers did not present the results as a reliable estimate of the current overall speedup. That is a useful warning against importing one percentage into a planning spreadsheet. It does not tell your team whether its current workflow is faster. Local measurement still needs clear task boundaries and an account of quality. I would compare a small set of accepted changes over several weeks, including the review and rework they required. The goal is to find where assistance helps, and where its output needs a different review process. Make a change easier to inspect An agent can prepare a useful review packet: the requirement it implemented, the behaviour that changed, the tests it ran, and the important things it did not verify. Each claim should point to an artifact the reviewer can inspect. “Tests pass” is less useful than the command, result, and relevant failure case. “No behaviour change” should be supported by a narrow diff and appropriate checks, rather than a confident paragraph. Keep the packet short enough to read. A thousand-word generated description can increase the review burden it was supposed to reduce. Limit work before adding reviewers If every developer can launch several coding tasks, the team needs an explicit limit on work awaiting review. Otherwise the system turns reviewer attention into an unbounded buffer. Finish a change before starting another one that depends on it. Split changes at meaningful behavioural boundaries. Route a high-risk change to the person who understands the failure mode, not merely the next available approver. A second model can help find suspicious code or missing cases. Its report is another input to review. It does not establish that the original agent’s assumptions were correct, particularly when both received the same incomplete specification. Watch the quiet costs Track how often a merged change needs a corrective follow-up, how long a reviewer spends reconstructing intent, and whether unfamiliar code is becoming harder to maintain. Those costs may appear weeks after the implementation time was saved. The useful leadership question is where the saved time went. If it went into better tests, smaller queues, and more considered design, the workflow is improving. If it went into starting more work than the team can examine, output has outrun the system that makes it dependable.
agent-memory-needs-delete-path: Suppose an assistant remembers that a service deploys to a particular region. The team moves the service. A month later, the assistant confidently prepares a change against the old region because the remembered fact still ranks well in retrieval. The memory was useful when it was written. Its usefulness had a lifetime that the storage system never recorded. Before adding a “remember this” tool, it is worth deciding how the agent will handle a fact that used to be correct. A memory is a claim with an owner A durable fact should carry its source, scope, observed time, and a way to check whether it is still valid. “Deploy to region A” is incomplete without the service, environment, and source revision. There is also a difference between a user preference and a system fact. A preference about response length can tolerate a lightweight correction path. A claim about production routing should be verified against the current deployment configuration before a write. I would keep these types separate in the data model. Their freshness rules, access controls, and consequences are too different for one generic confidence score. Expiry is a retrieval decision A time-to-live field is not enough if expired rows still enter the prompt. Apply expiry and access checks before selecting memory for context. Record why a candidate was rejected so that debugging does not require guessing which filter ran. For some facts, age is the wrong invalidation signal. A policy revision or repository commit is more precise. The useful question is whether the source that supported the claim has changed, not simply whether seven days have passed. Access also changes. A reader who could see a document last week may no longer be allowed to retrieve a summary of it. Rechecking permissions on the original document while serving its old summary from an unrestricted cache defeats the purpose of the check. Deletion has descendants One source document can produce a summary, several extracted facts, an embedding, a cached answer, and a handoff note. Deleting the source row leaves those descendants behind unless the system knows where they came from. Attach source identifiers to derived records. Maintain a reverse index from source to descendants. A removal request can then invalidate retrieval immediately and schedule physical cleanup of the remaining copies. For a small system, explicit lineage fields and a background job may be enough. The important requirement is that the cleanup can be checked. “We removed it from the vector store” says nothing about a summary already copied into another collection. Backups, audit records, and external exports need their own retention rules. Do not promise instant physical erasure from every copy unless the storage design can support it. The immediate guarantee may instead be that the material cannot be retrieved for new work. Test correction, not just recall A memory test suite should contain a fact, a correction to that fact, and a task that depends on the corrected value. Add a revoked source and a deleted source. Confirm that neither appears in the next context pack. Also test conflicting sources. The most recently observed text may be an outdated document that was re-imported yesterday. Observation time is not the same as the time a fact became true. The earlier living-knowledge essay asks how knowledge can accumulate usefully. This is the maintenance half of that question. A system that remembers everything but cannot reliably revise or remove anything becomes harder to trust with every successful ingestion. The context-pack showcase makes freshness and exclusion decisions inspectable. It is a small offline example, but the same question scales: what evidence permits this memory to participate in the next decision?
evaluate-the-state-not-the-story: Suppose a scheduling agent replies, “Your appointment is confirmed for Tuesday.” The database contains a reservation for Wednesday. The final message is concise, polite, and wrong in a way that matters. An evaluation that grades only the reply can miss this entirely. The state transition is the product. The sentence is its report. Anthropic’s January 2026 evaluation guide distinguishes an agent’s transcript from the final state of its environment. That distinction is a useful starting point for building tests that survive changes in prompting and model choice. Write the postcondition first For the appointment task, define success before running the agent: exactly one active reservation, for the requested customer, at the requested time, with no unauthorized notification recipients. Some checks are positive. The reservation must exist. Others are negative. No second reservation should have been created during a retry. Both belong in the grader. A final-answer assertion can still be useful. It might check that the agent does not claim success when the reservation is pending. It should not replace a query against the authoritative test state. Give the grader independent evidence A tool trace that says “reservation created” is evidence from the execution path being tested. If the same tool is broken, its trace and return value can agree while the database remains unchanged. Inspect the sandbox database or a separate test endpoint after the run. Keep the grader’s credentials and expected values outside the agent’s writable workspace. Otherwise the agent can accidentally modify its own exam, even without any intention to exploit it. For a coding task, this means preserving held-out tests or checking externally observable behaviour. A green test suite that the agent has just weakened deserves a different interpretation from an independently maintained acceptance suite. A clean fixture prevents a misleading pass Reset the environment for each trial. If yesterday’s reservation remains in the fixture, today’s failed agent might receive credit for it. If a previous trial exhausted a quota, the next trial might fail for an unrelated reason. Record the fixture revision, model configuration, tool version, and timeout policy with each result. These are part of the experiment. When one changes, the score no longer describes exactly the same system. For nondeterministic runs, keep the per-trial results. Three successes out of five is useful information. Averaging it into a rounded “quality score” can hide the fact that two users would have had no appointment. Keep policy failures visible Suppose an agent books the correct appointment but reads a different customer’s record on the way. A single success percentage has nowhere obvious to put that failure. Use separate fields for task completion, unauthorized access, duplicate effects, and cost. A release gate can require completion above a chosen threshold and zero observed unauthorized writes in the suite. Zero observed violations is still only a statement about those cases, not a proof of safety. The outcome-grader showcase runs four synthetic order fixtures. One contains a persuasive success message without a persisted order. Another contains a duplicate. It demonstrates the grading boundary without requiring a model subscription. Save the failures you can explain A failed trial is most useful when it leads to a reproducible case. Preserve a minimal fixture, the relevant trace, and the violated postcondition. Remove customer data before adding a production-derived example to the suite. Over time, that collection becomes a record of what the system has learned to handle. Its value comes from the specificity of the failures. A dashboard full of green circles cannot tell the same story.
approval-is-a-versioned-decision: Suppose an agent prepares an email to a supplier. A reviewer approves the draft. Before sending, the agent refreshes its context and changes the recipient list to include an external consultant. The workflow still has an approval flag. The action no longer matches the approved proposal. Every individual step looks reasonable, which makes the failure easy to miss. The reviewer clicked a real button. The agent used a real tool. The missing piece is an explicit relationship between the approved content and the eventual mutation. Store the decision, not just the click An approval record should identify the actor, tool, target, arguments, and expiry. It should also identify the revision of the evidence that made the proposal reasonable. For a database migration, that could include the schema revision and the inspected environment. For an email, it includes the recipient list and exact body. Compute a digest of a deterministic representation of the proposal. Before execution, reconstruct that representation and compare it with the approved digest. A changed recipient, amount, destination, or body requires a new decision. A digest provides equality checking. It does not prove who approved anything. The approval record still needs authenticated creation, protected storage, and an authorization check at execution time. Show the part that can hurt Approval interfaces often give the most space to the agent’s explanation. The dangerous part may be a single parameter hidden beneath it. Put the destination, scope, and irreversible effects next to the approval control. Make additions easy to distinguish from removals. If an operation affects 400 records, show the selection rule and a preview of the affected set. “Update customer records” is too vague to support a useful decision. There is a design tradeoff here. A large preview can overwhelm a reviewer. A tiny preview can conceal the consequence. Group changes by risk and make the highest-risk fields visible without expansion. Recheck the world at execution time Even unchanged arguments can become unsafe. A user’s access may have been revoked. An account may have entered a restricted state. A document revision may have changed the meaning of the proposed edit. Bind approval to a relevant version or precondition, then fail closed when it no longer holds. For an HTTP resource, a conditional update may provide that boundary. For a database, use a transaction with a version check. Where no atomic precondition exists, document the race instead of pretending that a preflight read eliminates it. MCP’s security guidance makes related distinctions around consent, client identity, and scope. An application still has to define the business action its own approval authorizes. Retries should preserve the receipt A single-use approval record is helpful, but consuming it before sending a request creates a recovery problem. A crash can leave a consumed approval and an unknown external outcome. Track execution separately from approval: proposed, approved, executing, completed, or uncertain. Pair the operation with a destination-supported idempotency mechanism where one exists. An uncertain result should enter reconciliation, not quietly mint another approval. The small approval-gate showcase demonstrates argument binding and replay rejection in memory. It deliberately leaves external execution out. That boundary keeps the example honest and makes the remaining production work visible. A useful approval system lets a reviewer answer one plain question after an incident: “Did this action match what I agreed to?” If answering requires reconstructing a conversation from fragments, the approval record is too weak.
mcp-stateless-business-state: A network connection disappears just after a tool accepts a request to create a support ticket. The client reconnects. Should it send the request again? That question survives every transport redesign. A protocol can tell the client how to communicate. Only the application can establish whether the ticket already exists. The MCP specification dated July 28, 2026 removes protocol-level sessions and the initialization handshake, moves protocol version and client capabilities into request metadata, and introduces server discovery. It also removes stream resumability. These are substantial changes for integration code. They do not make a business operation stateless. Put state where it can be recovered A ticket-creation workflow has at least three identities: the authenticated caller, the logical operation, and the individual network attempt. Combining them into a session ID makes recovery difficult. Give the logical operation a durable identifier before the first attempt. Bind it to the caller and a canonical description of the requested change. Each network retry can have a fresh request ID while referring to the same logical operation. For a hypothetical ticket service, the record might contain: operation: create-ticket-742 owner: support-team-a payload_digest: 08d1... state: accepted | executing | completed | uncertain result: ticket-918 The digest is there to reject accidental reuse of an operation ID with different arguments. It does not authenticate the caller. Authorization remains a separate check on every request. The uncertain state is worth keeping A timeout is not proof that an operation failed. The ticket may exist even though its acknowledgement never reached the client. If the downstream service supports an idempotency key, pass the logical operation identifier through according to that service’s contract. If it exposes a reliable lookup by external reference, reconcile against that reference. If it offers neither, record an uncertain outcome and escalate instead of blindly repeating the mutation. This costs some convenience. It also avoids teaching a recovery system to create duplicate work whenever it loses contact with the thing it is controlling. A local “sent” flag written before an external request cannot prove delivery. A flag written afterwards leaves a crash window. The destination’s semantics decide which guarantees are possible; a wrapper cannot manufacture exactly-once execution around an arbitrary API. Handles need owners and expiry The revised protocol allows application state to be represented through explicit handles. A handle is useful for a long-running export, but possession of its string should not automatically grant access to another customer’s export. Store the owner, creation time, expiry, and permitted operations with the handle. Recheck authorization when it is used. Decide what a client should see after expiration and what survives a server restart. These are application decisions that deserve tests alongside the happy path. Migrate with a failure matrix Before changing a gateway, test old and new client versions against the server versions you actually support. Include discovery failure, unsupported versions, a disconnect after acceptance, and a replay with changed arguments. The goal is to separate protocol compatibility from business correctness. A migration can pass every transport test and still duplicate a ticket on retry. Stateless transport is attractive because it reduces connection-specific machinery. The application should use that simplification to make its remaining state more explicit: who asked, what was accepted, what changed, and how a disconnected client can find out.
context-is-a-budget: Consider a support agent investigating a failed export. Its context contains the customer’s last twenty conversations, the complete API reference, three old incident reports, and a freshly retrieved permissions record. The permissions record is the only item that explains the failure. It occupies six lines near the bottom. Collecting more information has become a substitute for deciding what matters. The agent has plenty to read. Nobody has decided what deserves its attention. Anthropic’s context-engineering article describes context as a resource that needs active management across a run. The practical question for an application team is who owns those decisions, and how they can be inspected when an answer goes wrong. Start with the next decision For the export task, the next decision is whether the customer has permission to export this dataset. That calls for a current entitlement check, the dataset identifier, and the relevant policy. A discussion from six months ago about dashboard colours contributes nothing. I would give each workflow step a small context contract. It names the decision, required evidence, freshness rules, and a fallback when evidence is missing. This can be a typed object in code. It does not need another platform. { "decision": "may_export", "required": ["dataset_id", "current_entitlements", "export_policy"], "freshness": {"current_entitlements": "fetch_at_decision_time"}, "missing_evidence": "stop_and_request_access_check" } The contract also makes a useful review question possible: why is this particular document in the prompt? If the answer is merely that retrieval returned it, the selection policy needs work. Separate what must fit from what would be useful A context pack needs room for instructions, evidence, conversation, tool results, and the model’s response. Spending the entire allowance on retrieved text leaves the rest of the workflow competing for space. Reserve mandatory items first. Then choose optional material according to the current decision. Keep a manifest of included and excluded source IDs. An exclusion reason such as “superseded policy” is more useful than a silent truncation at an arbitrary character count. Token estimates also deserve honesty. A word count can support a rough offline demonstration. It cannot enforce a model’s actual context limit. Production admission should use the tokenizer or token-counting interface for the model being called, with room for tool schemas and response generation. A summary can lose the exception Suppose the original policy says that exports are allowed except for datasets under legal hold. A summary that says “exports are generally allowed” has removed the condition that matters most. For high-consequence decisions, preserve the exact governing clause and its source revision. Summarize background explanation more aggressively. These two kinds of text should not share the same compression policy. The handoff between agents needs similar care. Pass the selected dataset ID, checked policy revision, unresolved questions, and evidence references. A fluent paragraph about the investigation is pleasant to read, but it can hide which checks actually happened. Test the pack before testing the answer A useful test fixture contains an old policy that permits an action and a newer policy that denies it. Another contains a relevant document whose access was revoked. A third omits the required entitlement record entirely. Check which sources enter the pack before scoring the model’s reply. If the retrieval layer silently selects the old policy, changing the system prompt is an expensive way to debug a data-selection defect. The important output of context engineering is a defensible explanation of what the model was allowed to know at that moment. A smaller prompt may be a welcome side effect. The real benefit is being able to trace a decision back to the evidence that supported it.
ai-second-brain-living-knowledge: Everyone building an AI second brain starts in the same place. Dump everything in — notes, documents, chat logs, half-formed ideas — embed it, put it behind a retrieval layer, and let the model answer questions over it. For the first few weeks it feels magical. Then it starts to rot. The rot is not a bug. It is the predictable consequence of treating knowledge as a pile rather than a system. A pile grows. It does not learn. When you added a note in March saying your API rate limit was 100 requests per second, and another in June saying it is 500, the pile now contains both. Ask the second brain what your rate limit is and it will confidently tell you one of them — and you will not know which, or why. A second brain that only accumulates is a graveyard with good search. The interesting engineering — the part almost nobody builds — is in the verbs. How does it ingest ? How does it update ? And most consequentially, how does it resolve the moment two things it knows contradict each other? The Knowledge Is Already Scattered and Already Wrong If you have worked on any software team larger than three people, you already own a broken second brain. It is just spread across six tools that do not talk to each other. The onboarding steps live in a Confluence page last edited fourteen months ago. The actual setup steps live in a README that someone fixed but never backported to Confluence. The reason a config value is set to 30s and not 10s lives in a Slack thread that scrolled out of history. The decision to drop support for a legacy endpoint lives in a closed Jira ticket that nobody will ever find again. This is not a hypothetical failure of some future AI system. It is Tuesday on every engineering team on earth. The knowledge exists. It is simply un-reconciled — scattered across surfaces that each believe they are the source of truth, none of which agree. query: "how long is the payment webhook retry window?" CONFLUENCE "Architecture / Payments" "24 hours" · edited 2025-03-11 README.md services/payments/ "6 hours" · edited 2026-05-02 JIRA PAY-2841 (closed) "6h, was 24h" · 2026-04-28 SLACK #payments-eng thread "i think 12?" · 2026-06-19 naive second brain (embed all four, retrieve top-k) → returns "24 hours" — the Confluence page ranks highest, it is the longest and most authoritative-sounding → confidently wrong · the value changed to 6h a year ago reconciled second brain → returns "6 hours" · authority: PAY-2841 closed the decision · README corroborates → flags Confluence page as stale · surfaces the Slack guess as unverified The naive system does not just fail — it fails confidently , and it fails toward the most official-looking source, which on a real team is almost always the one nobody remembered to update. The Confluence page wins because it is long, formal, and well-embedded. The Jira ticket that actually changed the answer loses because it is terse and closed. This is the exact inversion of what you want, and no amount of better embeddings fixes it, because the problem is not retrieval. The problem is that four sources disagree and the system has no policy for deciding who is right. Every mechanism in the rest of this piece exists to solve the problem this one query exposes. Storage Is the Easy Part The reason most second-brain projects stall is that they optimize the one thing that was never hard. Vector search is a solved problem. You can stand up a semantic retrieval layer over ten thousand documents in an afternoon. What you cannot do in an afternoon is make that retrieval stay correct as the underlying knowledge shifts under it. The core insight is that a second brain is not a storage problem. It is a state reconciliation problem, and it looks far more like a distributed database with conflicting writes than it looks like a library. the metabolism of a second brain INGEST capture raw input — note, doc, transcript, clip — with provenance and timestamp DIGEST extract atomic claims — decompose prose into discrete, checkable assertions RECONCILE detect overlap with existing claims — merge, supersede, or flag contradiction SERVE answer queries from the reconciled state, not the raw pile — with citations FORGET decay or archive stale claims — a brain that never forgets drowns in noise Most implementations build INGEST and SERVE. The value lives in RECONCILE and FORGET. Notice that four of the five stages are about transformation, not storage. The pile-based approach collapses this into two — ingest and serve — and skips everything in the middle. That gap is where the rot lives. Claims Are the Right Unit The first architectural decision that matters is what you store. The naive answer is documents. The better answer is claims . A document is a container. "Meeting notes, June 12" is a document. It might contain twenty distinct assertions, some of which are decisions, some observations, some speculation, and some of which will be contradicted by next week's meeting. If your unit of knowledge is the document, you cannot reason about any of that. You can only retrieve the whole blob and hope the model sorts it out. A claim is atomic. "The Q3 launch is scheduled for September 15" is a claim. It is checkable, it has a truth value, it can be superseded, and it can conflict with exactly one other kind of thing — another claim about the Q3 launch date. When you make claims the unit, reconciliation becomes a tractable operation instead of a vibe. ANATOMY OF A CLAIM // claim record — the atom of the second brain { "claim_id" : "clm_a91f3c" , "subject" : "q3_launch.date" , // the addressable "slot" "assertion" : "September 15, 2026" , "confidence" : 0.9 , // ── PROVENANCE ─────────────────────────────────── "source" : "meeting_notes_2026-06-12" , "asserted_at" : "2026-06-12T15:04:00Z" , "author" : "alok" , // who said it — authority matters // ── LIFECYCLE ──────────────────────────────────── "status" : "active" , // active | superseded | disputed | archived "supersedes" : "clm_7e2b10" , // prior value for this slot "decay_after" : "2026-09-30" // event-dated claims expire } The subject field is the quiet hero here. It is a stable address — a slot — that multiple claims can compete for. Two claims with the same subject are, by definition, about the same thing, which means reconciliation only ever has to compare claims that share a slot. You never have to diff every claim against every other claim. You diff within a slot. This is what turns conflict detection from an $O(n^2)$ nightmare into something linear and cheap. Ingestion Is Extraction, Not Copying When a new document arrives, the wrong instinct is to chunk it and embed it. The right operation is to run it through a decomposition step that pulls out the atomic claims and normalizes each one onto a subject slot. In a real engineering stack, "a document arrives" means a webhook fires. A Confluence page is published, a Jira ticket transitions to Done, a pull request merges and changes a README, a markdown ADR lands in the docs/ folder, someone stars a message in Slack. Each connector emits a raw blob, and each blob is full of exactly the kind of prose that never survives contact with retrieval — "we discussed moving the retry window down, and after some back-and-forth agreed 6 hours makes more sense given the SLA." A pile embeds that whole sentence. A living brain extracts the one claim inside it — payments.webhook.retry_window = 6h — and throws the rest away. This is the single most important pipeline in the system, so it deserves to be explicit about its stages. ingestion pipeline — raw input to reconciled claims 1 segment split prose into candidate assertions — one idea per span 2 classify is this a fact, a decision, an opinion, or speculation? drop the noise 3 normalize to a subject slot "launch is Sept 15" and "we ship on the 15th" map to the same slot 4 probe the slot for existing claims does the brain already hold a claim about this subject? 5 route to reconciliation new slot → insert · same value → reinforce · different value → conflict Step three is where most of the intelligence lives and where naive systems fail. If "the launch is September 15" and "we're shipping on the 15th of Sept" do not resolve to the same subject slot, they will sit in the brain as two unrelated facts and never be compared. Slot normalization is the join key of the entire system. Get it wrong and reconciliation never fires. The Update Is a Reconciliation, Never an Overwrite Here is the discipline that separates a living second brain from a mutable key-value store: you never overwrite a claim . When new information arrives about a slot that already holds a value, you do not replace the old value. You supersede it, and you keep the old one, marked superseded , with a pointer forward. This is the same insight distributed systems reached decades ago with append-only logs. Overwriting destroys history, and history is exactly what you need when you later have to explain why the brain believes what it believes. A superseded claim is not garbage. It is the audit trail. slot: q3_launch.date — claim history 2026-04-02 clm_7e2b10 "August 30" superseded │ reason: date slipped after scope review 2026-06-12 clm_a91f3c "September 15" active query: "when does Q3 launch?" → September 15 (clm_a91f3c, from meeting_notes_2026-06-12) → note: revised from August 30 on 2026-06-12 The query response now carries something a pile can never offer — not just the current answer, but the fact that it changed , when, and from what. That single line of context ("revised from August 30") is often more valuable than the answer itself, because it tells the human that this is a moving target worth double-checking. Resolving Conflicts Is a Policy, Not a Guess The hard case is not a clean supersession where a newer claim obviously replaces an older one. The hard case is genuine conflict: two claims about the same slot, from different sources, where it is not obvious which is right. Your rate limit note from support says 100 rps. The API dashboard you screenshotted says 500. Which does the brain believe? The wrong answer is to let the model guess at query time. The right answer is to have a resolution policy that runs at reconciliation time and produces an explicit, inspectable decision. A second brain without a conflict policy is not neutral — it is silently arbitrary. conflict resolution — ordered policy ladder 1 authority — a claim from the system of record beats a claim from a note deterministic 2 recency — if authority ties, the more recently asserted claim wins deterministic 3 corroboration — three independent sources outweigh one, raise confidence deterministic 4 semantic judgement — LLM weighs specificity and plausibility, must cite reasoning model call 5 escalate — unresolvable → mark both disputed , surface to the human human Exhaust the cheap deterministic rules before spending a model call. Never skip straight to the guess. The ladder matters as much as its rungs. You climb it in order, stopping at the first rung that resolves the conflict. Most conflicts never reach the LLM — they are settled by authority or recency, which are cheap, deterministic, and auditable. The model is a fallback for genuine ambiguity, not the front line. And the final rung is the honest one: some conflicts cannot be resolved by the system at all, and pretending otherwise is worse than admitting it. A disputed claim shown to the user with both values is more trustworthy than a confident single answer that happens to be wrong. Authority is where you encode what your team actually knows about its own tools. In practice this is a ranked list of source types, and it is worth being blunt about it: for a config value, the code and its merged PR outrank everything — the repo does not lie about what is deployed. For a product decision, a closed Jira ticket or an accepted ADR outranks a wiki page. For process and onboarding, a recently-edited Confluence page outranks a stale README. And a Slack message, however recent, is a signal that something changed, not an authority on what it changed to — it should raise a flag for re-verification, never win a conflict on its own. Encoding this hierarchy once, explicitly, is what stops the second brain from trusting the most confident-sounding source instead of the correct one. Forgetting Is a Feature The last verb is the one that feels wrong to build. Every instinct says a second brain should remember everything. But a brain that treats a throwaway thought from two years ago with the same weight as yesterday's decision is not smart — it is cluttered. Signal degrades as noise accumulates. Forgetting in a second brain is not deletion. It is decay — a gradual reduction in retrieval priority based on age, access frequency, and claim type. An event-dated claim ("the launch is September 15") becomes irrelevant the moment the event passes and can be archived automatically. A reference fact ("our primary region is us-east-1") has no natural expiry and should persist until superseded. A fleeting note that was never accessed again drops in priority until it stops surfacing in results — still stored, still auditable, but no longer competing for the model's attention. decay behavior by claim type reference fact no decay — persists until explicitly superseded event-dated auto-archive once the date passes — irrelevant by definition frequently used access resets the clock — used knowledge stays warm never revisited priority decays on a half-life — sinks out of results, never deleted The design principle is that forgetting adjusts visibility , not existence . Nothing is destroyed, because the audit trail is sacred. But the brain's working attention is finite, and spending it on stale noise is the same mistake as an over-eager cache holding onto data nobody wants. Serving From the Reconciled State All of this machinery exists to make the final step trustworthy. When a query arrives, the brain does not retrieve from the raw pile of documents. It retrieves from the reconciled layer — the current, active claims — and it answers with citations back to provenance. This is the payoff. The answer to "what's my API rate limit?" is no longer a coin flip between two contradictory notes. It is the active claim on the api.rate_limit slot, resolved by policy, carrying its source and its history. If the claim is disputed, the brain says so. If it was recently revised, the brain says that too. The retrieval is not smarter — the state it retrieves from is simply correct , because the hard work happened at write time, not read time. That is the whole thesis. A pile does its thinking at read time, every time, badly. A living second brain does its thinking once, at write time, and banks the result. Reconciliation is not overhead. It is the entire product. The Broader Point We keep trying to build second brains out of storage and search because those are the parts that are easy to buy. But knowledge is not a static asset that appreciates by accumulation. It is a living thing that contradicts itself, goes stale, and demands maintenance. The organ that manages that maintenance — that ingests, reconciles, forgets, and can always explain itself — is the actual second brain. The vector store is just its filing cabinet. The engineers who have run production databases will recognize every idea here, because none of them are new. Append-only logs, superseding writes, conflict resolution policies, cache eviction, provenance and audit trails — we solved these for data decades ago. What is new is the recognition that a second brain is not a knowledge base you read from. It is a knowledge base you must constantly, carefully, write to. The intelligence was never in the recall. It was always in the reconciliation.
agents-survive-failure-checkpointing: Every agentic system I have seen fail in production fails the same way. Not because the LLM made a bad decision, not because a tool returned an unexpected result, but because the agent had been running for four minutes, had completed twelve of its fifteen steps, and then a network timeout killed the process. Restarting meant starting from zero. The team called it a retry. What it actually was was a confession that the system had no memory of its own work. This is the statefulness problem — the most consequential and least discussed failure mode in production agentic AI. We spend enormous energy making agents smarter, faster, cheaper. We spend almost none making them durable. The engineering disciplines that solve this — checkpointing, state capsules, and resumability — are borrowed from distributed systems and adapted for the unique challenges of LLM-driven workflows. They are not exotic. They are table stakes for any agent that runs longer than a single API call, touches more than one external system, or operates in an environment where partial failure is not a theoretical edge case. It is not a theoretical edge case. It is Tuesday. Why Agents Are Stateless by Default The root cause is architectural. Most agentic frameworks are built around a request-response model. A user sends a message. The agent produces a response. The session ends. This model is inherited from the LLM inference API itself — every call to the model is independent. State is maintained, if at all, by passing the full conversation history in the context window on each call. This works for chat. It fails catastrophically for long-running tasks. A long-running agent is not a chat session. It is a workflow — a sequence of decisions and actions that collectively accomplish a goal over minutes or hours. When such a workflow fails at step 12 of 15, the naive recovery strategy is to restart at step 1. This is not just inefficient. It is dangerous. Some steps are not idempotent. If step 3 was "send a confirmation email" or "charge the customer's card" or "provision the infrastructure," restarting from zero does not undo those actions. It repeats them. task_order_42817 — execution trace 14:28:33.104 FETCH customer order history ✓ 124ms 14:28:34.231 INFER classify order intent (LLM) ✓ 1.2s 14:28:35.444 EMIT send confirmation email ✓ 82ms ← side-effect 14:28:35.528 VERIFY inventory check × 3 SKUs ✓ 340ms 14:28:36.012 WRITE create ERP record ✓ 217ms ← side-effect 14:28:36–14:32:45 ··· steps 6–11 completed 14:32:46.003 CALL payment processor API ············· ✗ ETIMEDOUT after 30.0s · process killed · PID 23841 exit 1 without checkpointing → cold restart at 14:28:33 · 11 steps re-executed → confirmation email sent again · ERP record duplicated with checkpointing → capsule loaded in 187ms · resume at step 12 → email: skip (ledger entry found) · ERP: skip (ledger entry found) The problem is not just efficiency. It is correctness. A stateless agent in a world of non-idempotent operations is a liability. What Agent State Actually Contains Before designing a checkpointing system, you need to be precise about what "agent state" contains. This is not obvious. Agents are not simple state machines with a single integer counter. Their state is a composite of at least four distinct layers, each with different persistence requirements and different semantics on recovery. agent state — four layers L1 EXECUTION current step index · plan structure · step outputs · pending queue must persist L2 MESSAGES full message history · tool call records · model responses · token counts costly to rebuild L3 LEDGER every external mutation: emails sent · APIs called · records written · files created safety-critical L4 CONTEXT fetched docs · resolved schemas · env vars · upstream data with TTL may go stale Most implementations persist L1+L2. The ones that skip L3 are the ones that send duplicate emails. The side effect ledger deserves special attention. Most checkpointing implementations focus on execution state and conversation history — they ignore the ledger. This is the mistake that causes duplicate emails and double-charged payments. Before any resumption logic runs, the first thing the system must check is: "What did this agent already do?" The ledger makes that question answerable. State Capsules A state capsule is the structured artifact that captures agent state at a specific point in execution, sufficient to resume the agent from that point without re-running completed steps or repeating side effects. The key word is sufficient . A state capsule is not a complete dump of everything. That is a backup. A capsule is the minimal representation that enables faithful resumption — designed to be small enough to write cheaply and frequently, but complete enough that resumption is correct. ANATOMY OF A STATE CAPSULE // capsule: state_capsule_v1 { "capsule_id" : "cap_7f3a9b" , // globally unique, immutable "task_id" : "task_order_42817" , "created_at" : "2026-06-20T14:33:07Z" , "schema_version" : 3 , // ── EXECUTION STATE ────────────────────────────── "plan" : { steps: [...], current_index: 11, total: 15 }, "step_outputs" : { 0: {...}, 1: {...}, ... 10: {...} }, // ── SIDE EFFECT LEDGER ─────────────────────────── "effects" : [ { "type" : "email_sent" , "to" : "customer@..." , "step" : 2 }, { "type" : "erp_record_created" , "id" : "ERP-9921" , "step" : 7 } ], // ── CONTEXT SNAPSHOT ───────────────────────────── "context" : { fetched_at: "...", data_hash: "sha256:...", ttl_s: 900 }, // ── INTEGRITY ───────────────────────────────────── "checksum" : "sha256:e3b0c44298..." } Three design choices here are worth explaining explicitly. schema_version — Capsules will outlive your code. When you deploy a new agent version, you will have capsules in storage written by the old version. The schema version field lets your resumption logic detect version mismatches and decide whether to upgrade the capsule, reject it, or restart the task. If you omit this field, you will regret it within three sprints. data_hash on context — External data fetched at the start of a task can change. If a capsule contains a stale snapshot of a customer record that has since been updated, resuming from it may produce incorrect results. The hash lets you detect staleness on resumption and decide whether to re-fetch or proceed with the snapshot. checksum on the capsule itself — Capsules stored in external systems can be corrupted. A checksum over the capsule body lets you detect corruption before attempting resumption, preventing the agent from operating on invalid state. When to Checkpoint Knowing what to save is only half the problem. The other half is knowing when. Checkpoint granularity is a tradeoff between: Recovery overhead : coarser checkpoints mean more re-work on resumption Write overhead : finer checkpoints mean more storage I/O during execution Semantic correctness : some checkpointing boundaries are natural (after a tool call completes) while others are dangerous (inside an LLM reasoning step) checkpoint timing — what boundaries are valid ● after every tool call — tool calls carry side effects; record completion before proceeding always ● after plan generation — planning is expensive; a task in progress should never re-plan from scratch always ◐ after LLM reasoning — idempotent but costly; checkpoint when output exceeds ~2K tokens if > 2K tok ◐ on elapsed time — catches long-running steps that have no natural boundary every 60s ○ inside LLM token generation — generation is atomic; no valid partial output exists to serialize never The last row matters. You cannot checkpoint an LLM mid-generation. There is no valid "partially generated response" that you can resume. The unit of checkpointing must be at the boundary between agent steps — never inside one. The Resumption Decision Detecting that a capsule exists is not the same as knowing what to do with it. When an agent restarts and finds a capsule, it must make a series of decisions before resuming execution. ResumptionCoordinator — decision sequence 1 capsule found for task_id load from store, deserialize 2 verify checksum corrupt → cold restart + alert valid → continue 3 check schema_version mismatch → migrate or cold restart matches → continue 4 check context data_hash + TTL stale → re-fetch, update capsule fresh → continue 5 resume from checkpoint skip completed steps · skip recorded ledger effects · execute from current_index This decision tree should be implemented as a dedicated ResumptionCoordinator — a component separate from the agent's planning and execution logic. Mixing resumption decisions into execution logic is how teams end up with subtle correctness bugs: agents that resume from a valid capsule but then re-execute a side effect because the ledger check was in the wrong place. Before and After The concrete difference checkpointing makes is best understood as a timeline comparison. execution cost — 15-step task, failure at step 12 STATELESS AGENT — two full passes steps 1–11 ✗ re-run 1–11 (wasted · side effects repeat) 12–15 ✓ total compute: ~26 steps 2× side effects restart latency: full CHECKPOINTED AGENT — skip completed work steps 1–11 + capsules ✗ load 12–15 ✓ total compute: ~15 steps no duplicate effects resume latency: ~200ms at 800ms avg per step: 8.8s wasted per failure event · at scale this is measurable infrastructure cost The numbers here are not hypothetical. In a workflow with fifteen steps, each costing 800ms on average, the difference between a cold restart and a capsule resume is 8.8 seconds of wasted execution time — on every failure. At production scale, with hundreds of concurrent agent tasks, this compounds into measurable cost and latency differences. Implementation Patterns The Checkpoint Decorator The simplest way to add checkpointing to an existing agent step function is through a decorator that handles capsule writes automatically. The step implementation stays clean; durability is a cross-cutting concern. @checkpoint(task_id=task.id, step_index=11) async def process_payment(ctx: AgentContext) -> PaymentResult: result = await payment_gateway.charge( amount=ctx.order.total, customer_id=ctx.customer.id ) ctx.effects.record("payment_charged", result.transaction_id) return result The decorator writes a capsule before the function executes (recording the intent) and updates it after (recording the completion and output). If the process dies between intent and completion, the resumption logic can detect an incomplete step and decide whether to retry or flag for human review. The Idempotency Key For side effects that must not be duplicated, the pattern is to generate a deterministic idempotency key derived from the capsule ID and step index, and pass it to every external API call. idempotency_key = f"{capsule.capsule_id}:step:{step_index}" await stripe.charges.create( amount=order.total_cents, idempotency_key=idempotency_key, # Stripe deduplicates on this customer=customer.stripe_id ) Combined with the side effect ledger, this creates a two-layer defense: the ledger prevents the agent from re-attempting a step at all, and the idempotency key handles the case where the step was attempted but the response was not received before failure. The Capsule Store Interface Capsule storage should be abstracted behind an interface to allow swapping backends without changing agent logic. The minimum interface is five operations: class CapsuleStore(Protocol): async def write(self, capsule: StateCapsule) -> None: ... async def read(self, task_id: str) -> StateCapsule | None: ... async def delete(self, task_id: str) -> None: ... async def list_incomplete(self) -> list[str]: ... async def gc_expired(self, max_age_hours: int) -> int: ... The list_incomplete method is essential for operational recovery: it lets a background worker find all tasks that were interrupted (capsule exists but not marked complete) and enqueue them for resumption. Without this, interrupted tasks require manual intervention to recover. What Good Observability Looks Like A checkpointing system without observability is half-built. The signals that matter: Capsule write latency — If capsule writes are slow, they add overhead to every step. Alert if p95 > 50ms. Resumption rate — What percentage of task starts are resumptions vs cold starts? A spike here indicates a systemic failure upstream. Effect ledger collision rate — How often is the ledger preventing a duplicate side effect? This should be non-zero (that means it's working) but low. Stale context rate — How often are capsules resumed with context that has expired its TTL? High rates indicate tasks are being interrupted and not retried promptly. Capsule garbage collection lag — Completed tasks should have their capsules cleaned up. Growing storage is a sign GC is not running. The Broader Point The impulse in AI engineering is to solve reliability problems by making the model smarter. Use a better reasoning model, write a more precise prompt, add more validation. These are real improvements. But they do not change the fundamental fact that agents run in environments where things fail: networks time out, APIs return 503s, processes get killed, context windows overflow. Durability is not a model capability. It is an infrastructure discipline. Checkpointing, state capsules, and resumability are the mechanism by which you transform an agent from a fragile one-shot executor — which succeeds perfectly in demos and fails silently in production — into a durable worker that can be interrupted, recovered, inspected, and resumed with confidence. The distributed systems engineers reading this will recognize the pattern immediately. We solved this problem for queues, workflows, and distributed databases decades ago. The ideas — write-ahead logs, idempotency keys, at-least-once delivery with deduplication — are not new. What is new is applying them rigorously to the execution substrate of LLM-driven agents. The agents that will survive production are not the smartest. They are the ones that know how to survive failure, resume from the last good state, and never do the same work twice.
learning-loop-architecture: Every significant AI deployment I have worked on eventually reveals the same structural pattern: there are not one but two compounding feedback loops running simultaneously, and the organizations that recognize this early build systems that get exponentially better. Those that do not plateau, spending more on tokens while getting less back. I call this the Learning Loop Architecture — a framework for designing AI systems that compound in both human capability and machine intelligence at the same time, rather than trading one for the other. The Two Loops The core insight is deceptively simple. Every AI system in production generates two distinct streams of value, each feeding back into itself: Human Capital Loop weeks → months Engineers interact → Build judgment → Better design → Richer outputs ↩ invisible in dashboards · compounds judgment · slow but dominant Token Capital Loop hours → days Outputs evaluated → Fine-tune & RAG → Better model → Higher quality signal ↩ highly measurable · compounds data · where most teams over-invest The Human Capital Loop Engineers interact with AI systems. They learn what works and what fails. That learning improves how they design prompts, architect pipelines, structure evaluations, and select tools. Better human judgment leads to better system design, which produces better outputs, which generates richer learning opportunities. The humans compound. This loop operates on a timescale of weeks to months. It is invisible in dashboards. It does not show up in token costs or latency metrics. But it is the dominant factor in whether an AI program succeeds or stagnates over a twelve-month horizon. The Token Capital Loop AI systems process inputs and produce outputs. Those outputs get evaluated — by humans, by automated evals, by downstream system behavior. Evaluation data feeds back into fine-tuning, prompt refinement, RAG index updates, and routing logic improvements. Better data produces better models and retrieval, which produce better outputs, which generate higher-quality evaluation signal. The models compound. This loop operates on a timescale of hours to days. It is highly measurable. It shows up in eval scores, cost-per-query, and user satisfaction metrics. It is where most teams focus their engineering effort — and that is precisely the problem. Why Both Loops Must Run in Parallel The failure mode I see most often: teams invest heavily in the Token Capital Loop — automated evals, fine-tuning pipelines, sophisticated prompt engineering frameworks — while allowing the Human Capital Loop to atrophy. Engineers become operators rather than architects. They tune parameters without building intuition. They optimize metrics without understanding failure modes. The result is a system that improves on benchmarks but becomes increasingly fragile. When the operating environment shifts — a new model version, a change in user behavior, a regulatory requirement — there is no accumulated human judgment to draw on. The team cannot adapt because they never developed the muscle. The inverse failure mode is rarer but equally damaging: teams that invest in human understanding but never build the infrastructure to capture and compound machine learning. They have brilliant engineers who manually improve things, but nothing compounds automatically. Every improvement requires the same human effort as the last one. They scale linearly while competitors scale exponentially. How the Loops Couple Human Loop judgment · intuition deposits insight ↓ Shared Knowledge Graph Token Loop data · performance ↓ draws examples Multiplicative Compounding Human insight shapes what the system optimises for. System quality accelerates human learning. uncoupled: 5.3× (additive) coupled: ~4.66× per loop (multiplicative) Architectural Patterns for the Learning Loop Pattern 1: The Instrumented Apprenticeship Design your AI systems so that every human interaction with the system generates structured learning signal — not just for the model, but for the human. When an engineer corrects an agent's output, the system should capture what was wrong (Token Loop), but the workflow should also surface why the agent made that mistake (Human Loop). Expose the reasoning trace. Show the retrieval context. Make the failure legible. Concretely: every correction event should produce a ticket-sized artifact that includes the input, the agent's reasoning chain, the retrieved context, the output, and the human's correction with rationale. This artifact feeds the Token Loop through fine-tuning data, and the Human Loop through pattern recognition. Pattern 2: Rotation Through the Evaluation Layer The engineers who build AI systems should regularly rotate through evaluating their outputs. Not as a chore, but as an architectural practice. The fastest way to build judgment about what an AI system is actually doing — as opposed to what metrics say it is doing — is to read its outputs critically, at volume, regularly. I have seen teams where the evaluation function is entirely automated or delegated to a separate QA team. Those teams consistently make worse architectural decisions because they have no visceral understanding of how their system behaves at the edges. Pattern 3: The Shared Knowledge Graph Build an explicit, queryable knowledge base that captures what the team has learned about AI system behavior. Not tribal knowledge in Slack threads — structured, searchable documentation of failure modes, effective patterns, model-specific quirks, and domain-specific prompt strategies. This is the shared substrate between the two loops. The Human Capital Loop deposits knowledge here; the Token Capital Loop can draw on it for few-shot examples, retrieval context, and evaluation criteria. It is the bridge that allows human learning to directly accelerate machine learning and vice versa. Pattern 4: The Compounding Flywheel Review Every two weeks, explicitly review both loops. Ask: what did our humans learn that we have not yet encoded into the system? What has the system learned that our humans have not yet internalized? The gap between these two is where compounding stalls. In practice this looks like a review meeting with two fixed agenda items: (1) what patterns have we noticed in failures or successes that should inform system design, and (2) what has changed in system behavior that the team should understand and adapt to. The Compounding Math Here is why this matters quantitatively. Assume each loop compounds at 5% per cycle independently. Over 20 cycles: Token Loop alone: 1.05^20 = 2.65x improvement Human Loop alone: 1.05^20 = 2.65x improvement Both loops coupled: The improvement is not additive (5.3x) but multiplicative with interaction effects. In practice, I observe something closer to 1.08^20 = 4.66x because the loops amplify each other. Human insight accelerates the Token Loop; machine output quality accelerates the Human Loop. Compounding Divergence Over 40 Cycles cycle 5 cycle 10 cycle 20 cycle 30 cycle 40 Single loop (5%/cycle) Coupled loops (8%/cycle) Over 40 cycles the gap becomes dramatic. This is why organizations that get the Learning Loop Architecture right early develop seemingly insurmountable advantages within 18 months. Anti-Patterns to Watch For The Automation Trap Automating away all human touchpoints eliminates the input signal for the Human Capital Loop. Every interaction you automate should be evaluated: is this removing a rote task (good) or removing a learning opportunity (dangerous)? The Metrics Mirage Token Capital Loop improvements are easy to measure. Human Capital Loop improvements are hard to measure. The result: teams systematically under-invest in the hard-to-measure loop. Combat this by tracking leading indicators of human learning — number of novel failure modes identified, diversity of evaluation strategies applied, speed of adaptation when system behavior changes. The Solo Genius When AI system knowledge concentrates in one or two people, the Human Capital Loop has a bus factor of one. The architecture should be designed so that learning is distributed, not concentrated. Pair rotations through the evaluation layer. Shared knowledge graphs. Explicit teaching moments in code review. Implementation Checklist For teams starting to think about this deliberately: Instrument every human correction to capture both the fix and the reasoning Build a structured knowledge base for AI system behavior patterns Rotate engineers through evaluation at least one day per sprint Review both loops explicitly every two weeks Track human learning indicators alongside machine performance metrics Design automation to preserve, not eliminate, human learning surfaces Ensure AI system knowledge is distributed across at least three engineers The Longer View The organizations that will dominate the AI era are not those with the best models or the most tokens. They are those that build architectures where human and machine intelligence compound together. The Learning Loop Architecture is not a framework you implement once — it is a design philosophy that shapes every decision about how humans and AI systems interact in your organization. The question is not whether your AI system is getting better. The question is whether your team is getting better at the same rate. If the answer is no, you have a compounding problem — and it will catch up with you faster than you think.
agentic-ai-harness-engineering: Every team building agentic AI hits the same wall. The prototype works beautifully in a demo — the agent reasons, calls tools, produces correct outputs. Then you ship it. Within hours, you discover that the LLM hallucinates a tool name, retries infinitely, loses state mid-conversation, or silently degrades in quality with no signal that anything is wrong. The difference between that prototype and a production system is not a better model. It is the harness — the engineered control plane that wraps, constrains, monitors, and recovers the agent through every failure mode the real world will throw at it. I call this discipline harness engineering : the systematic design of the non-LLM infrastructure that makes agentic systems reliable, observable, and safe at scale. It is the most under-discussed and under-invested layer in the agentic AI stack, and it is the layer that determines whether your system survives contact with production traffic. What Is an Agent Harness? An agent harness is the orchestration substrate that sits between your application logic and the LLM. It is responsible for everything the model cannot be trusted to do reliably: managing state across turns, enforcing execution policies, handling failures gracefully, collecting telemetry, and ensuring the agent operates within defined boundaries. Anatomy of an Agent Harness APPLICATION LAYER Business logic, user interface, API endpoints AGENT HARNESS STATE MACHINE Turn management Context windowing Memory persistence EXECUTION POLICY Max retries Timeout enforcement Cost ceilings RECOVERY ENGINE Fallback chains Circuit breakers Graceful degrade TOOL REGISTRY Schema validation Permissions Rate limits EVALUATION LAYER Output quality Guardrails Drift detection TELEMETRY Latency + cost Trace correlation Anomaly signals LLM PROVIDER OpenAI · Anthropic · Local Models · Routers The critical insight is that every component above the LLM layer is deterministic, testable, and under your control. The LLM is the only non-deterministic element — and the harness exists precisely to contain that non-determinism within safe operational boundaries. The Six Pillars of Harness Engineering After building and operating production agent systems across multiple domains, I have converged on six pillars that every serious harness must implement. Skip any one of these and you will discover the gap in production — usually at the worst possible time. Six Pillars of Harness Engineering 01 STATE MANAGEMENT Turn tracking, context windowing, memory persistence, checkpoint/restore 02 EXECUTION POLICY Retry budgets, timeout enforcement, cost ceilings, concurrency limits 03 RECOVERY ENGINE Fallback model chains, circuit breakers, graceful degradation, dead-letter queues 04 TOOL GOVERNANCE Schema validation, permission boundaries, rate limiting, parameter sanitisation 05 EVALUATION LAYER Output quality scoring, guardrail checks, semantic drift detection, regression alerts 06 OBSERVABILITY Structured traces, cost attribution, quality metrics, anomaly detection, SLA tracking Pillar 1: State Management — The Agent's Memory Architecture The most common failure mode in production agents is state corruption. The agent loses track of where it is in a multi-step task, re-executes steps it already completed, or hallucinates that it did something it never actually did. This happens because most agent frameworks treat state as an afterthought — a growing list of messages with no structure. A production harness implements state as an explicit, typed state machine with well-defined transitions: Agent State Machine IDLE user_input PLANNING plan_failed plan_ready RECOVERY retry → PLANNING EXECUTING tool calls + LLM exec_failed / eval_fail exec_success EVALUATING gate checks + quality scoring eval_pass COMPLETE Every transition logged Max dwell timeout per state Deterministic — LLM cannot override Every state transition is logged. Every transition has a maximum dwell time (timeout). The state machine enforces that the agent cannot skip steps, cannot execute without planning, cannot complete without evaluation. This is not a suggestion to the LLM — it is deterministic code that the LLM cannot override. The context window strategy is equally critical. A naive implementation passes the entire conversation history to every LLM call. A production harness implements sliding-window context with semantic compression: recent turns are passed verbatim, older turns are summarised, and irrelevant tool outputs are pruned. The agent always has the context it needs without the token bloat that degrades both quality and cost. Pillar 2: Execution Policy — Budgets, Bounds, and Backpressure An unconstrained agent is a liability. Without execution policies, a single confused agent can retry a failing API call indefinitely, burn through your entire token budget in minutes, or spawn cascading tool calls that overwhelm downstream services. Execution policy is the set of hard constraints that define the operational envelope: Execution Policy Configuration POLICY: research-agent-v2 RETRY BUDGET per_tool 3 per_turn 5 backoff exp 1s on 5xx, timeout TIMEOUTS llm_call 30s tool_exec 60s per_turn 120s task_total 600s COST CEILING per_turn 50K tok per_task 200K tok hourly $2.00 breach degrade CONCURRENCY parallel_tools 3 pending_tasks 10 max_turns 15 on_limit yield Hard stops enforced by harness infrastructure — not guidelines, not prompts. These are not guidelines — they are hard stops enforced by the harness. When an agent hits a cost ceiling, the harness does not ask the agent what to do. It downgrades to a cheaper model, or pauses and escalates to a human, or terminates the task with a structured error. The agent has no say in this. That is the point. The most important execution policy is the turn limit . Agents in unbounded loops are the number one cause of cost blowouts in production. A well-designed harness enforces a maximum turn count per task and, when that limit is reached, forces the agent to summarise its progress and yield — either to a human or to a supervisor agent that can decide whether to allocate more budget. Pillar 3: Recovery Engine — Designing for Failure LLMs fail. They fail in ways that are hard to predict and hard to distinguish from correct behaviour. A production harness treats failure as the default assumption and designs every path with recovery in mind. The recovery engine implements three patterns: Recovery Pattern Hierarchy ! FAILURE DETECTED R RETRY Same model, fresh context window success → continue exhausted F FALLBACK Cheaper model, simplified prompt degraded → continue exhausted C CIRCUIT BREAK Stop calling, preserve state, cooldown → human escalation Fallback chains are the most underutilised pattern. When GPT-4o times out or produces garbage, you do not retry with GPT-4o. You fall back to Claude Sonnet with a simplified prompt. If that fails, you fall back to a template-based response that at least preserves correctness. The user gets a degraded but functional response instead of an error. The quality degradation is logged, and the system self-heals when the primary model recovers. Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures. If a tool endpoint returns errors on three consecutive calls, the harness opens the circuit — it stops calling that tool entirely for a cooldown period. This prevents the agent from burning retries against a downed service, protects downstream systems from thundering herds, and gives the infrastructure time to recover. Checkpoint/restore is the safety net. Before every tool execution, the harness checkpoints the full agent state. If the tool call corrupts the conversation or the agent enters an unrecoverable state, you restore to the last good checkpoint and try an alternative path. This is not theoretical — it is essential for any agent that makes external writes (sending emails, creating tickets, deploying code). Pillar 4: Tool Governance — The Agent's API Contract Tools are the agent's hands. Without governance, those hands can do anything — including things the agent was never designed to do. Tool governance is the layer that ensures every tool call is valid, authorised, bounded, and audited. A governed tool registry provides four guarantees: Schema validation: Every tool call is validated against a strict JSON schema before execution. If the LLM hallucinates a parameter, the call is rejected before it reaches the tool — not after. Permission boundaries: Tools are scoped to the current task context. A research agent cannot access write tools. A summarisation agent cannot access network tools. This is enforced by the harness, not by the prompt. Rate limiting: Each tool has per-minute and per-task call limits. An agent cannot spam an API endpoint regardless of what the LLM decides to do. Parameter sanitisation: All tool parameters are sanitised for injection attacks. SQL parameters are parameterised. Shell commands are escaped. URLs are validated against allow-lists. Tool Call Lifecycle LLM Output: call search_docs(query='...') 01 Parse tool name + parameters 02 Schema validation fail → reject + retry 03 Permission check fail → reject + log 04 Rate limit check fail → queue 05 Parameter sanitisation 06 Checkpoint current state 07 Execute tool timeout → fallback 08 Validate output schema 09 Log trace span (tool, params, duration, cost) 10 Return structured result to LLM The key architectural decision is that the harness — not the LLM — determines which tools are available for a given turn. You can dynamically narrow the tool set based on the agent's current state. In the PLANNING state, only read-only tools are available. In the EXECUTING state, write tools become accessible. This state-dependent tool availability eliminates entire categories of agent misbehaviour. Pillar 5: Evaluation Layer — Continuous Quality Assurance You cannot run an agent in production without knowing whether its outputs are good. But "good" is hard to define for free-form language generation. The evaluation layer solves this by applying multiple lightweight checks at runtime — not just during development. A production evaluation layer operates at three levels: Runtime Evaluation Stack GATE CHECKS (per-turn, blocking) Format compliance — does output match expected schema? Guardrail pass — no PII leakage, no harmful content, no policy violations? Factual grounding — are claims supported by retrieved context? QUALITY SCORING (per-task, non-blocking) Relevance score against user intent. Completeness — did the agent address all parts of the request? Coherence — is the multi-turn conversation logically consistent? DRIFT DETECTION (aggregate, async) Rolling quality percentiles — is p50 quality declining over the last hour/day? Behavioural drift — is the agent using tools differently than its baseline? Cost drift — is token consumption trending upward without corresponding quality gains? Gate checks are blocking — if an output fails a gate check, the harness rejects it and forces the agent to regenerate. Quality scores are non-blocking — they are logged and used for alerting and continuous improvement. Drift detection runs asynchronously over aggregated data, looking for systemic degradation that per-request checks would miss. The most valuable evaluation metric I have found in practice is the regeneration rate : what percentage of agent outputs are rejected by gate checks and regenerated? A healthy agent regenerates less than 5% of outputs. When regeneration exceeds 15%, something fundamental has changed — a model update, a prompt regression, or a shift in input distribution — and the system alerts operators to investigate. Pillar 6: Observability — The Nervous System Observability for agentic systems is qualitatively different from traditional application monitoring. You are not just tracking request latency and error rates. You are tracking reasoning quality, decision coherence, tool utilisation patterns, and cost efficiency — metrics that have no direct equivalent in conventional software. A production harness emits structured traces that capture the full decision chain: Agent Trace Schema TRACE: task_7f2a total: 3,160ms planning 420ms 1.2K tok model: gpt-4o · plan_steps: 4 · confidence: 0.87 tool: search_docs 890ms score: 0.72 params: {query: "...", limit: 10} · results: 7 docs tool: search_docs RETRY #1 650ms score: 0.89 reason: low_relevance · params: {query: "...", limit: 20} · results: 12 docs generation 1,200ms 3.4K tok model: gpt-4o · gate_check: PASS · quality: 0.91 tokens: 4,600 cost: $0.023 turns: 2 tools: 2 (1 retry) This trace gives you everything: latency breakdown per phase, token consumption per call, quality scores, retry reasons, and total cost attribution. You can aggregate these traces to build dashboards that answer the questions that matter: which tasks are expensive and why? Which tools fail most often? Is quality trending down after the last prompt change? Which user queries consistently trigger recovery paths? Harness Patterns for Multi-Agent Systems When you move from single agents to multi-agent architectures, the harness becomes even more critical. You are now managing not just individual agent behaviour but inter-agent communication, coordination protocols, and system-level properties that emerge from agent interactions.
